items.question: When should errors found during spot-checking trigger escalation to exhaustive review of the full batch?

options.A: Escalation should be triggered any time the spot-check sample size exceeds the planned size
options.B: Escalation should be triggered when any output in the spot-check is longer than the reviewer expected
options.C: Escalation should be triggered when the model used hedging language in any spot-checked item
options.D: Escalation should be triggered when spot-check errors are systematic — recurring across a category of claims rather than appearing as isolated, random occurrences

items.question: What does an internally consistent model output that contains an external factual error demonstrate about the relationship between coherence and accuracy?

options.A: Internal consistency and factual accuracy are independent properties — a model can produce coherent but factually wrong output
options.B: An internally consistent output containing a factual error proves the model's calibration is poor
options.C: Internal consistency checking is redundant for outputs that have been verified against external sources
options.D: A factually wrong but internally consistent output must have originated from a stale source rather than a hallucination

items.question: Which TWO conditions together indicate that model output on a topic is at elevated risk from both hallucination and staleness simultaneously? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The topic changes frequently in the real world, meaning training-time knowledge may already be outdated
options.B: No current source documents were provided in context, leaving the model reliant on parametric memory for all claims
options.C: The model used hedging language throughout the response, signalling widespread calibration uncertainty
options.D: The output is longer than the reviewer's typical review capacity per session
options.E: The topic appears frequently in the model's training data, giving it well-developed patterns for assertive responses

items.question: Which verification approach is most appropriate for high-stakes output on a domain where the model's parametric knowledge is known to be unreliable or rapidly outdated?

options.A: Ask the model to generate the output multiple times and select the most consistent response across runs
options.B: Require all specific claims to be traced to current, authoritative source documents provided in context or confirmed against independent sources before use
options.C: Apply a higher-tier model to reduce the error rate before conducting sampling-based verification
options.D: Increase the number of items on the review checklist to cover more potential error categories for this domain

items.question: What does it mean to 'close the loop' between verification findings and prompt improvement in a model workflow?

options.A: Storing verified correct outputs in Project knowledge so the model learns from them in future sessions
options.B: Asking the model to revise any outputs that failed verification before they are discarded
options.C: Using patterns found in verification failures to identify and fix prompt or instruction deficiencies that caused those failures
options.D: Notifying all output consumers when a previously verified output is later found to contain an error

items.question: Which TWO practices together constitute a comprehensive verification approach for a multi-source synthesis, addressing both commission and omission errors? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Comparing each specific claim in the synthesis against its stated or implied source to confirm it is accurately represented
options.B: Asking the model to identify which source document each claim came from before any verification begins
options.C: Reading each source document and confirming that all material findings from that source appear in the synthesis
options.D: Applying a readability metric to confirm the synthesis meets the target reading level and audience register
options.E: Asking a second model to summarise the same sources and comparing the two model summaries for consistency

items.question: When model output is used as input to a second model or automated process, what verification step should occur before passing the output downstream?

options.A: The downstream model should be prompted to flag any claims in the input that it cannot reproduce from its own parametric memory
options.B: The first model should generate the output twice to confirm consistency before it is passed downstream
options.C: The second model will detect and correct errors in the first model's output as part of its own generation process
options.D: Human verification of the first model's output should be completed before it is used as input to the downstream process, because errors propagate and may compound in multi-stage pipelines

items.question: What is the key distinction between evaluating a model workflow and verifying a specific model output, as they relate to improvement decisions?

options.A: Workflow evaluation assesses systematic performance across many outputs and informs whether the workflow should be changed; output verification confirms whether a specific item is correct and informs whether it should be used
options.B: Workflow evaluation is performed before deployment; output verification is performed after deployment — they serve the same function at different project phases
options.C: Workflow evaluation is automated; output verification requires human judgment — they are the same activity performed by different actors
options.D: Workflow evaluation measures cost and latency; output verification measures accuracy — they address different properties of the same workflow

items.question: A model output contains both grounded claims traceable to uploaded source documents and ungrounded claims from parametric memory, mixed together. What is the most important first verification step?

options.A: Check all claims against the model's training data to identify which are parametric in origin
options.B: Identify which claims are grounded and which are ungrounded, so verification effort can be directed appropriately — grounded claims require source-checking, ungrounded claims require source-finding
options.C: Reject the entire output and re-prompt with explicit instructions to use only the provided source documents for all claims
options.D: Ask the model to label each claim as grounded or ungrounded before verification begins

items.question: What specific risk arises from setting the escalation threshold too high — requiring a large proportion of sampled errors before triggering full batch review?

options.A: A high threshold substantially increases the total number of items the reviewer must check before a decision is reached
options.B: A high threshold causes reviewers to flag minor formatting issues that do not warrant escalation decisions
options.C: Errors occurring below the threshold may cause significant harm in a large batch because the absolute error count is high even at a low percentage rate
options.D: A high threshold prevents the organisation from building a useful record of batch error rates for benchmarking over time

items.question: Which two properties must both be confirmed for verification to be considered complete for a specific factual claim?

options.A: The claim must include hedging language and the source must be present in the context window
options.B: The claim must be internally consistent with adjacent claims and stylistically appropriate for the intended audience
options.C: The claim must be shorter than a specified length limit and must include a citation to a named source
options.D: The claim must be accurate relative to its source, and the source must itself be authoritative and current

items.question: Which TWO properties distinguish a formal evaluation from a spot-check when the purpose is deciding whether to change a model workflow? (Choose TWO)

options.A: A formal evaluation uses a statistically determined sample sized to detect the minimum error rate of concern at a specified confidence level
options.B: A spot-check is always performed by the person who authored the prompt; a formal evaluation is always performed by an independent reviewer
options.C: A formal evaluation uses defined quality criteria and a representative test set, enabling quantified performance comparisons before and after workflow changes
options.D: A spot-check produces no written findings; a formal evaluation always produces a written report that can be shared with stakeholders
options.E: A formal evaluation is performed only before deployment; a spot-check is always reactive, performed only after an error is reported

items.question: Which TWO statements correctly describe the relationship between grounding, calibration, and accuracy in producing reliable model output? (Choose TWO)

options.A: A claim can be grounded and inaccurate if the source it traces to is itself wrong
options.B: Good calibration ensures that grounded claims are also accurate because the model knows which sources to trust
options.C: High accuracy can be achieved without grounding if the model's parametric memory happens to be correct on the relevant topic
options.D: Grounding makes a claim auditable but does not guarantee accuracy; accuracy additionally requires that the source is correct and the model represented it faithfully
options.E: A well-calibrated model will always hedge on ungrounded claims, making grounding detectable from the output text alone

items.question: What factor should most directly govern how strict an acceptance threshold is applied to a Claude output?

options.A: Output length, since longer outputs contain more opportunity for compounding errors.
options.B: Model tier used, since higher-tier models warrant less stringent review.
options.C: Number of prior iteration cycles the prompt has undergone.
options.D: The stakes of the decision or action the output will directly inform.

items.question: How does calibration differ from accuracy in evaluating model output?

options.A: Accuracy measures whether claims are grounded in context; calibration measures whether they are factually true.
options.B: Calibration applies only to probabilistic or numeric outputs; accuracy applies to all claim types.
options.C: Accuracy concerns whether a claim is true; calibration concerns whether expressed confidence matches the probability the claim is true.
options.D: A well-calibrated output is necessarily accurate; an accurate output may not be well-calibrated.

items.question: What distinguishes a sycophantic response change from a genuinely helpful concession?

options.A: A helpful concession is driven by new information or a valid argument; sycophancy is driven by the user's emotional tone or persistence alone.
options.B: Sycophancy occurs only when the model changes a factual claim; helpful concession involves tone or framing only.
options.C: A helpful concession is always accompanied by an explicit explanation of what changed; sycophantic agreement is silent.
options.D: Sycophancy is a property of single-turn responses; helpful concession occurs across multiple conversation turns.

items.question: What is the key functional distinction between an acceptance criterion and a rubric dimension?

options.A: Acceptance criteria are defined before generation; rubric dimensions are defined after reviewing the output.
options.B: An acceptance criterion establishes a binary pass/fail threshold; a rubric dimension provides a scored scale allowing gradations of quality.
options.C: Acceptance criteria apply to the output as a whole; rubric dimensions apply to individual sentences or claims.
options.D: A rubric dimension can be subjective; acceptance criteria must always be objective and measurable.

items.question: Which TWO conditions are appropriate escalation triggers when reviewing Claude output? (Choose TWO)

options.A: The output will directly inform a decision that is irreversible once acted upon.
options.B: The output required more than two rounds of iterative refinement before reaching its current form.
options.C: The output contains a claim the reviewer cannot verify that is material to a consequential section.
options.D: The output's tone deviates from brand voice guidelines by a marginal but noticeable degree.
options.E: The output was produced using a lower model tier than the team's standard template specifies.

items.question: When is rejecting and restarting preferable to editing a Claude output?

options.A: When the output exceeds the target word count by more than ten percent.
options.B: When more than one factual claim requires verification before use.
options.C: When the output uses a different structural format than the prompt specified.
options.D: When the output's core reasoning or structure is fundamentally flawed such that surface edits cannot address the root problem.

items.question: Which TWO scenarios exemplify internal logical inconsistency rather than a factual error? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Claude states the capital of Australia is Sydney.
options.B: Claude recommends Option A as the lower-risk choice in section two, then recommends Option B as the lower-risk choice in the conclusion without explanation.
options.C: Claude attributes a well-known quotation to the wrong author.
options.D: Claude reports a statistic that was accurate at training time but has since changed.
options.E: Claude describes a project as on-track in the executive summary and at risk in the status section of the same document.

items.question: Which TWO describe a correct use of a golden set in output evaluation? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Comparing new outputs against golden examples to detect quality regression after a prompt change.
options.B: Inserting golden outputs as few-shot examples in the prompt to steer the model's generation style.
options.C: Treating golden outputs as factual ground truth to verify the accuracy of new outputs.
options.D: Establishing a baseline quality level that reviewers use as a reference when scoring new outputs.
options.E: Storing golden outputs in Project knowledge so Claude retrieves and replicates them automatically.

items.question: What type of reasoning error occurs when Claude applies the correct formula but uses inconsistent or mismatched units?

options.A: Internal inconsistency, because the output contradicts itself about how the calculation was performed.
options.B: Hallucination, because the incorrect result was generated rather than retrieved from a reliable source.
options.C: Unit error, because the computational framework was correct but the measurement dimensions were misapplied.
options.D: Calibration failure, because the model expressed confidence in a result derived from flawed inputs.

items.question: What is the primary purpose of conducting a bias review of Claude's output?

options.A: To identify systematic skews in how groups, perspectives, or options are represented or characterized.
options.B: To verify that the output does not contain any claims that exceed the model's training knowledge.
options.C: To confirm that the output's tone is neutral and does not favor one communication style over another.
options.D: To check whether the model's hedging language is applied consistently across all claims.

items.question: What does tone compliance mean in the context of output quality review?

options.A: The output contains no language that could be interpreted as emotionally charged or persuasive.
options.B: The output's register, voice, and style match the expectations defined for the intended audience and use case.
options.C: The output hedges every claim to avoid projecting false confidence to the reader.
options.D: The output is free from all grammatical errors and follows standard editorial conventions.

items.question: How do completeness and accuracy differ as output evaluation properties?

options.A: Completeness applies to factual claims; accuracy applies to structural and formatting requirements.
options.B: Accuracy is evaluated against external reference sources; completeness is evaluated against prior outputs for the same task.
options.C: Completeness and accuracy are equivalent — an incomplete output is also inaccurate by definition.
options.D: Completeness measures whether all required elements are present; accuracy measures whether the elements present are correct.

items.question: When is a 'good enough for purpose' acceptance standard most appropriate for Claude output?

options.A: When the output will be used in a regulated filing and the team wants to save review time.
options.B: When the cost of a quality error is low relative to the cost of additional review and the output will be human-reviewed before any consequential use.
options.C: When the model tier used is known to produce reliable output on this class of task.
options.D: When previous versions of the same output received positive feedback from end users.

items.question: How does a self-consistency check differ from external verification when reviewing Claude output?

options.A: Self-consistency checks are performed by a different reviewer; external verification uses automated tools.
options.B: Self-consistency checks are faster because they require no domain expertise; external verification requires a subject-matter expert.
options.C: A self-consistency check detects internal contradictions within the output; external verification compares claims against authoritative sources outside the output.
options.D: Self-consistency checks apply to numeric outputs only; external verification applies to all claim types.

items.question: What mechanism produces sycophantic behavior when a user disagrees with Claude's initial response?

options.A: The model updates its position based on the social signal of displeasure rather than on new information or a valid counter-argument.
options.B: The model loses access to earlier context in a long conversation and cannot maintain its original reasoning.
options.C: The model interprets user disagreement as evidence that its initial response was factually wrong and corrects accordingly.
options.D: The model applies a safety filter that prevents it from maintaining positions that users explicitly contest.

items.question: Why are internal contradictions more difficult to detect in long outputs than in short ones?

options.A: Long outputs are more likely to contain arithmetic errors that compound into contradictions.
options.B: Long outputs usually involve multiple authors, increasing the chance that different sections contradict each other.
options.C: Reviewers may not apply a rubric to long outputs because the scoring process takes too long.
options.D: The contradicting claims may be far apart in the document, making it harder for a reviewer to hold both in working memory simultaneously.

items.question: What is the primary goal of a fairness review applied to Claude output?

options.A: To confirm that the output does not contain any legally prohibited language.
options.B: To assess whether the output treats comparable groups, options, or perspectives with consistent standards and depth.
options.C: To verify that the output does not express any opinions that could conflict with organizational policy.
options.D: To ensure the output uses inclusive language as defined in the organization's style guide.

items.question: What should a reviewer primarily assess when checking Claude output for brand compliance?

options.A: Whether the output cites the organization's published products and services correctly.
options.B: Whether the output contains any factual claims that conflict with the organization's official positions.
options.C: Whether the output's voice, terminology, and stylistic choices align with the organization's defined brand standards.
options.D: Whether the output was generated using the prompt template approved by the organization's marketing team.

items.question: Which TWO are components of a structured bias review of Claude output? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Checking whether comparable groups or options receive equivalent depth and scrutiny in the output.
options.B: Verifying that all factual claims in the output can be traced to documents in the context window.
options.C: Confirming that the output's tone matches the register specified in the prompt.
options.D: Identifying loaded or asymmetric language that characterizes some subjects differently than comparable ones.
options.E: Checking that the output does not exceed the word count specified in acceptance criteria.

items.question: What distinguishes acceptance criteria from output format specifications?

options.A: Acceptance criteria define whether the output meets the task's quality requirements; format specifications define how the output should be structured or presented.
options.B: Acceptance criteria apply only to subjective quality dimensions; format specifications address objective, measurable requirements.
options.C: Format specifications are defined before generation; acceptance criteria are applied after the output is reviewed.
options.D: Acceptance criteria are established by the evaluator; format specifications are embedded in the prompt by the user.

items.question: What condition most strongly disqualifies applying a 'good enough for purpose' acceptance standard?

options.A: The output was produced on the first generation attempt without iterative refinement.
options.B: The output is longer than typical for this class of task.
options.C: The output will reach its audience without an additional human review step before use.
options.D: The prompt that generated the output has not been previously validated on similar tasks.

items.question: What is the distinction between output consistency and output correctness in evaluation?

options.A: Consistency concerns whether the output follows the specified format; correctness concerns whether the content is accurate.
options.B: Consistency measures whether repeated runs on the same input produce equivalent outputs; correctness measures whether any individual output is accurate.
options.C: Consistency and correctness are equivalent — an output that is inconsistent with prior runs is by definition incorrect.
options.D: Correctness applies to factual outputs; consistency applies to stylistic and tonal outputs.

items.question: How does calibration differ from precision in characterizing model output quality?

options.A: Precision measures how narrow and specific a claim is; calibration measures whether specific claims are more accurate than general ones.
options.B: Calibration and precision are synonyms in output evaluation — both describe how closely the model's output matches the true value.
options.C: Precision describes the granularity or specificity of a claim; calibration describes whether the confidence attached to claims matches their actual correctness rate.
options.D: Calibration is a property of numeric outputs; precision applies to all output types.

items.question: Which TWO statements correctly distinguish a rubric from a golden set in output evaluation? (Choose TWO)

options.A: A rubric is defined before generation; a golden set is assembled after reviewing multiple generated outputs.
options.B: A rubric provides scored quality dimensions; a golden set provides reference examples of what high-quality output looks like.
options.C: A rubric is a scoring framework used by reviewers; a golden set is a collection of expert-validated input-output pairs used as a comparison standard.
options.D: A rubric applies only to text outputs; a golden set can include any output modality.
options.E: A rubric measures one output at a time; a golden set requires comparing at least ten outputs simultaneously.

items.question: A Claude output states a factually correct claim as settled consensus when expert opinion is genuinely divided. Which failure is present?

options.A: Overconfident tone, because the confidence expressed exceeds what the state of expert agreement warrants, even though the claim itself is accurate.
options.B: Hallucination, because stating a contested claim as consensus generates false impressions regardless of the underlying fact.
options.C: Sycophancy, because the model likely adopted the user's framing of the claim as settled in order to align with their apparent view.
options.D: Internal inconsistency, because claiming consensus where none exists contradicts the actual distribution of expert opinion within the same domain.

items.question: When should a reviewer escalate an output for additional expert review rather than reject it and regenerate?

options.A: When the output contains format errors that cannot be corrected through direct editing.
options.B: When the output's quality score on the evaluation rubric falls below the median expected for this task type.
options.C: When the reviewer has already attempted two iterations without achieving acceptable quality.
options.D: When the output may be acceptable but the reviewer lacks the domain expertise to make that determination independently.

items.question: Which TWO statements correctly distinguish completeness from accuracy as evaluation dimensions? (Choose TWO)

options.A: Completeness is evaluated against the task's requirements; accuracy is evaluated against external facts or expert knowledge.
options.B: An incomplete output is always also inaccurate because missing elements misrepresent the full picture.
options.C: An output can achieve full completeness while containing inaccurate claims, and can be fully accurate on what it covers while being incomplete.
options.D: Completeness applies only to structured outputs such as reports; accuracy applies to all output types.
options.E: Completeness is a more objective dimension than accuracy because requirements can be enumerated while truth is harder to verify.

items.question: Which TWO correctly distinguish a fairness review from a bias detection check in output evaluation? (Choose TWO)

options.A: A fairness review assesses only tone and language choice; bias detection examines content and coverage.
options.B: A fairness review assesses whether the output treats comparable subjects evenhandedly; bias detection identifies systematic skews that may originate in the model's training patterns.
options.C: Bias detection is automated and tool-assisted; fairness review is always performed manually by a human expert.
options.D: Fairness review focuses on the output's treatment of comparable groups or options relative to each other; bias detection may identify skews even when all groups receive similar treatment if that treatment reflects a training artifact.
options.E: A fairness review is only necessary when the output explicitly discusses demographic groups; bias detection applies to all output types.

items.question: What problem does over-hedging in a Claude output create for the reader?

options.A: It causes the model to omit claims it is uncertain about, producing an incomplete output.
options.B: It destroys the uncertainty signal by treating all claims as equally uncertain, so the reader cannot prioritize which claims to verify.
options.C: It makes the output harder to read by adding redundant clauses that reduce readability.
options.D: It indicates that the model's confidence calibration is generally accurate on this task.

items.question: What makes a golden set stale, and why is a stale golden set a quality risk?

options.A: A stale golden set contains outputs that scored below the current acceptance threshold, so comparisons produce misleadingly low scores.
options.B: A stale golden set was generated by an older model version, so it cannot reliably predict the quality of newer model outputs.
options.C: A stale golden set lacks sufficient variety, causing reviewers to over-focus on one class of output.
options.D: A stale golden set was curated against requirements that have since changed, so comparisons now validate against an outdated standard rather than the current one.

items.question: What is rubric gaming in the context of output evaluation?

options.A: Optimizing a prompt to produce outputs that score well on the rubric's defined dimensions without necessarily improving real-world usefulness.
options.B: Assigning inflated scores to outputs to avoid the work of regenerating and reviewing them again.
options.C: Using a rubric from a different task type when no purpose-built rubric exists for the current output.
options.D: Reviewing an output multiple times with the same rubric to produce a more reliable average score.

items.question: Why is sycophancy particularly difficult to detect when it occurs across multiple conversation turns?

options.A: Later turns reference the same context documents, making it appear that evidence exists for the new position.
options.B: Multi-turn conversations usually involve different reviewers for each turn, creating a continuity gap.
options.C: The model's revised position often includes new reasoning that makes the shift appear principled rather than socially driven.
options.D: Sycophancy is suppressed by safety filters in early turns but not in later turns of the same conversation.

items.question: What is the primary risk when an arithmetic error occurs in an intermediate step of a multi-step calculation?

options.A: The model will flag the error through reduced confidence on subsequent steps.
options.B: The error propagates into all downstream steps that depend on the wrong intermediate value, compounding the inaccuracy.
options.C: The model will restart the calculation from the beginning to maintain internal consistency.
options.D: The error is confined to the intermediate step and does not affect the final output if the remaining steps are correct.

items.question: What quality failure is present when Claude reverses its recommendation between turns without any new information being introduced?

options.A: Calibration failure, because the model's confidence in its recommendation clearly exceeded the underlying evidence.
options.B: Internal inconsistency, because the model's output across turns contradicts itself within the same conversation thread.
options.C: Hallucination, because at least one of the two recommendations must have been generated without factual basis.
options.D: Sycophancy, because the reversal driven by social cues rather than new evidence is the defining characteristic of sycophantic behavior.

items.question: When does expressing uncertainty in a Claude output represent a calibration failure rather than appropriate caution?

options.A: When the model hedges claims that are well-established and verifiable, creating false doubt about reliable information.
options.B: When the model uses hedging language in outputs that will be read by non-expert audiences.
options.C: When the model hedges in areas where it has been specifically instructed to be assertive.
options.D: When the model hedges factual claims but not its stylistic or tonal choices.

items.question: What is the primary limitation of relying on Claude's self-critique to verify factual accuracy?

options.A: Self-critique requires access to an external search tool that is not available in all Claude interfaces.
options.B: Self-critique is computationally expensive and significantly increases response time.
options.C: The model may reproduce the same factual error on the critique pass that it produced on the generation pass.
options.D: Self-critique can only detect errors in the most recent message, not in earlier turns of the conversation.

items.question: What risk does an over-permissive acceptance criterion introduce into an output review workflow?

options.A: It causes reviewers to reject otherwise acceptable outputs, increasing regeneration cost unnecessarily.
options.B: It allows substandard outputs to pass review and reach downstream users, potentially causing harm or requiring costly correction.
options.C: It makes the rubric dimensions redundant because all outputs meet the binary threshold regardless of rubric score.
options.D: It increases the variance of outputs that pass review, making quality prediction less reliable.
